Task and constraints: Given an array of non-negative integers nums, you are initially positioned at the first index of the array. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Scans positions while maintaining the farthest reachable index and the end of the current jump layer. When the scan crosses the current layer end, it counts a jump and advances that layer; an index beyond farthest reach returns -1.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy reachability layers count minimum jumps; each layer is expanded to the farthest position seen.
Invariant: reachable is the farthest index seen so far; curr_reachable marks the end of the layer covered by jump_count.
Edge cases: The statement guarantees reachability, though this code returns -1 if that assumption is broken. A single value returns zero jumps.
Complexity: The author labels time O(n) and space O(1); O(n) time and O(1) extra space; each index is visited once and only scalar state is stored.

Task and constraints: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all the possible permutations. You can return the answer in any order. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Returns list(permutations(nums)), delegating permutation generation to itertools and materializing all results.
Technique and why it applies: A library permutation iterator enumerates every ordering of the input; converting it to list stores all permutations.
Invariant: The iterator yields arrangements using the input elements; the returned list contains every generated ordering.
Edge cases: An empty input yields one empty permutation under itertools semantics; repeated values may yield duplicate arrangements because no deduplication is done.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. There are n! outputs of length n, so time and output space are at least O(n*n!).

Task and constraints: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all the possible permutations. You can return the answer in any order. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: DFS chooses each current element, recurses on a newly sliced list excluding that element, and extends the path. At an empty remainder it appends the path object to results.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking explores every choice order; slicing removes the chosen occurrence from later choices.
Invariant: Each path contains chosen elements in order, and nums contains the remaining elements.
Edge cases: For empty input the base case appends an empty path; slices and path concatenations allocate copies. The result stores path objects.
Complexity: The author labels O(n^2*n!) time and O(n^2) space; slicing/copying at each branch adds overhead, while storing all results costs O(n*n!).

Task and constraints: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all the possible permutations. You can return the answer in any order. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Uses a used-array and mutable current path. It selects each unused element, recurses, then pops and marks it unused again; a copy is saved when path length equals input length.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking systematically enumerates all permutations while the used flags prevent reusing an index in one arrangement.
Invariant: At each recursive call, cur contains exactly the chosen elements and used marks those same input positions.
Edge cases: Empty input records one empty permutation; repeated values at distinct indices create duplicate value sequences because this variant does not skip duplicates.
Complexity: The author labels O(n*n!) time and O(n) space; traversal state is O(n), but the returned permutations require O(n*n!) output space.

Task and constraints: Given a collection of numbers, nums, that might contain duplicates, return all possible unique permutations in any order. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Recursively permutes the tail, then inserts the first value into each existing permutation at positions before its first equal value and at the equal value's position.
Technique and why it applies: Insertion-based construction grows permutations by placing each next value into existing arrangements.
Invariant: Each res entry contains the processed suffix's values, and insertion adds the removed head exactly once.
Edge cases: The special case handles one element; the code has no explicit empty-list base case, so empty input recurses indefinitely. Duplicate handling depends on finding the first equal value.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. The number of permutations is factorial; repeated list copies and insertion make time/output costs large, with recursion depth O(n).

Task and constraints: Given a collection of numbers, nums, that might contain duplicates, return all possible unique permutations in any order. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Starts with one empty partial arrangement. For each input value, it inserts that value at every position in each current arrangement, keeping a candidate only if it is not already in next.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative insertion constructs permutations and explicit membership checks remove duplicate arrangements.
Invariant: After each outer iteration, solutions contains unique permutations of the processed prefix.
Edge cases: Repeated input values are deduplicated by list membership, but candidate not in next scans accumulated results and is costly.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Candidate generation is factorial with linear-list duplicate checks that can add another factorial factor; result storage is O(n*n!).

Task and constraints: Given a collection of numbers, nums, that might contain duplicates, return all possible unique permutations in any order. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Sorts the values, then backtracks using a used array. It skips a duplicate value when its previous equal value has not been used in the current path; complete paths are copied to results.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted backtracking plus duplicate-order pruning emits each distinct value permutation once.
Invariant: cur is a prefix of a permutation and used marks its positions; equal values are selected in a canonical order.
Edge cases: Empty input reaches the completion condition and returns one empty arrangement. Sorting mutates nums; duplicate values are handled by the skip rule.
Complexity: The author labels O(n*n!) time and O(n) space; traversal state is O(n), while all output permutations require O(n*n!) space.

Task and constraints: Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in any order. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: For each string, sorts its characters and uses that sorted string as a dictionary key, appending the original string to that group. It returns the dictionary's group lists.
Technique and why it applies: A canonical sorted-character key groups strings with the same character multiset.
Invariant: Every string is stored under a key made from exactly its sorted characters.
Edge cases: Empty strings share the empty key; input order within groups is retained in one variant. Sorting each string dominates work.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. If strings have length L and there are N strings, time is O(N*L log L); the map stores all strings plus keys.

Task and constraints: Implement pow(x, n), which calculates x raised to the power n (i.e., x^n). The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Stores x on the object, handles exponent zero, converts negative n to a positive exponent, recursively halves even exponents and reduces odd exponents by one, then takes the reciprocal if needed.
Technique and why it applies: Exponentiation by squaring reduces even powers quickly; odd powers peel off one factor.
Invariant: pow(n) returns x raised to n for positive n, with even cases squaring the half-power.
Edge cases: x=0 with a negative exponent divides by zero; recursion uses true division n/2, so float exponents are passed recursively in Python and can affect depth/precision.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Intended time is O(log |n|), but the odd branch reduces n by one before halving, and recursion uses O(log |n|) depth for positive integers; implementation's `/` produces floats.

Task and constraints: The n-queens puzzle is the problem of placing n queens on an n x n chessboard such that no two queens attack each other. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Places one queen per row. The DFS tracks used columns and the two diagonal identifiers, and records a column list when all rows are assigned; the final comprehension converts each placement into board strings.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking prunes any square sharing a column or diagonal with an existing queen.
Invariant: col_per_row has one safe column per completed row; the sets/lists track forbidden columns and diagonals.
Edge cases: n=1 returns a one-queen board; no solutions yields an empty list. The code stores diagonal trackers as lists, so membership checks are linear.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Search is factorial/exponential in n with pruning; list-based membership and copied tracker lists add overhead, and returned boards require O(n^2) per solution.

Task and constraints: The n-queens puzzle is the problem of placing n queens on an n x n chessboard such that no two queens attack each other. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Backtracks row by row, using sets for occupied columns and both diagonal identifiers. It increments a shared count when row reaches n and removes each placement from the sets after recursion.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking tries each column and rejects conflicts in constant-average-time set lookups.
Invariant: The sets contain exactly the columns and diagonals occupied by queens already placed in prior rows.
Edge cases: The base case counts a complete board once; cleanup after recursion restores the prior state. n=1 yields one arrangement.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Search is exponential/factorial with O(n) active placement state; set operations are expected O(1).

Task and constraints: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum and return its sum. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Defines a memoized recursive Kadane function: F[i] is the best subarray sum ending at i, either nums[i] alone or the previous best plus nums[i]. It evaluates the last index and returns max(F).
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming over prefixes stores the best subarray ending at each index.
Invariant: F[i] equals the maximum sum of a nonempty subarray ending exactly at i.
Edge cases: All-negative arrays return their largest element, not zero. The code assumes nums is nonempty because it sets F[0]. Recursion depth can reach n.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n) with memoization; space is O(n) for F and up to O(n) recursion depth.

Task and constraints: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum and return its sum. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: For each value, updates curr to the better of starting a new subarray here or extending the previous subarray, then updates the global best.
Technique and why it applies: Kadane's algorithm maintains the best subarray ending at the current position.
Invariant: curr is the maximum sum of a nonempty subarray ending at the current element; result is the best seen so far.
Edge cases: All-negative arrays are handled by initializing to negative infinity. The code assumes nonempty input.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space, consistent with one pass and two scalar values.

Task and constraints: Given an m x n matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Uses four boundaries and walks each layer with open-ended loops, handling the remaining row or column separately to avoid duplicated corner cells.
Technique and why it applies: Boundary simulation follows the spiral's top, right, bottom, and left edges.
Invariant: The boundaries delimit the unvisited inner rectangle after each layer.
Edge cases: The code accesses matrix[0], so an empty matrix fails. Single row/column cases rely on its special branches; unusual rectangular cases should be checked carefully.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(m*n) because each cell is appended once; output is O(m*n), despite no separate working structure.

Task and constraints: Given an m x n matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Walks the top row, right edge, bottom row in reverse, and left edge in reverse, then moves all boundaries inward until they cross.
Technique and why it applies: Layer-by-layer boundary traversal follows spiral order.
Invariant: The boundary variables enclose the cells not yet traversed.
Edge cases: An empty outer matrix returns []; a matrix with zero columns is not explicitly guarded. Conditions prevent repeated bottom/left edges in narrow layers.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and O(1) space; traversal state is constant, excluding the O(m*n) output list.

Task and constraints: You are given an integer array nums. You are initially positioned at the array's first index, and each element in the array represents your maximum jump length at that position. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Scans positions from left to right, immediately failing if an index is beyond the reachable boundary. It expands the boundary and exits early once the last index is reachable.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy reachability checks whether each scanned position can be reached and extends the frontier.
Invariant: reachable is the farthest position reachable from all positions processed so far.
Edge cases: A zero at the frontier can make later indices unreachable; a single element succeeds. The commented-out DFS is not executed.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n), space O(1), because the active code performs one scan with scalar state.

Task and constraints: You are given an integer array nums. You are initially positioned at the array's first index, and each element in the array represents your maximum jump length at that position. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Scans indices while they are within the farthest reachable boundary and updates that boundary with i+length; finally checks whether the boundary reaches the last index.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy reachability keeps only the farthest index attainable from the scanned prefix.
Invariant: reachable is the farthest index reachable from any index scanned so far.
Edge cases: A one-element array returns true. Zero jumps may stop progress; the method correctly returns false if the last index stays beyond reachable.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space, consistent with one pass and a scalar boundary.

Task and constraints: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [starti, endi], merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input. The input and required output follow the problem statement.
Idea: Sorts intervals by their starts, then appends disjoint intervals or merges overlaps into the last output interval by extending its end.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting followed by a sweep makes overlaps adjacent and easy to merge.
Invariant: result holds merged intervals for all input intervals processed so far.
Edge cases: Touching intervals merge because a start equal to the prior end is not greater. Sorting mutates the input; output entries may alias input intervals.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n log n) for sorting plus O(n) scanning; auxiliary storage is O(n) for result, despite the author label if present.
